10.text: E. Westermarck, quoting from W. Hooper, mentions that among the

11.text: Chukchee (Tuski), repudiated wives, with their children, are to a certain extent

12.text: supported by their former husbands.¹ W. Hooper, however, speaks about

13.text: those wives who have been put aside for some new favorite, and mentions

14.text: that it was considered a duty of the man to afford a home and sustenance

15.text: for such wives, as well as for the children by them.² In such cases the mar-

16.text: riage is not dissolved. Nevertheless I would call even this statement some-

17.text: what exaggerated. Of course, a Chukchee husband who has more than one

18.text: wife may be inclined to prefer the younger one, and to neglect the older

19.text: one. I knew of cases where neglect like this gave rise to jealousy and strife

20.text: between the wives. On the other hand, several husbands who were in a similar

21.text: position mentioned that they considered themselves obliged to visit their wives

22.text: in turn, one after the other. “Otherwise there would be trouble,” they said.

23.text: And really the national character of the Chukchee is such, that the complete

24.text: neglect of a wife, especially if she has children, would give occasion for trouble

26.text: At the same time W. Hooper acknowledges that “repudiation” is quite

27.text: another thing than such neglect. Directly after the passage quoted above he

28.text: says, “But repudiation is perfectly recognized, and in instances of misconduct,

29.text: and sometimes of dislike, put in force without scruple or censure. In these

30.text: cases the rejected wife returns to her father’s or brother’s lodge, and, unless

31.text: of a very bad character, does not generally wait long for another husband;

32.text: very often returning to her original spouse, to be perhaps again discarded.”

34.text: In the majority of cases, however, the initiative in breaking up the mar-

35.text: riage comes from the bride’s family, which retains its hold on the woman for

36.text: five or six years, even if the latter has meanwhile borne two children. In

37.text: case of friction between the two families, that of the bride takes the woman

38.text: back, by force if necessary. Of course, it is not the old fathers who most

39.text: ardently support that custom, but the elder brothers, especially if they are

40.text: numerous. Occasionally, when the woman loves her husband and refuses to
